lesson_title: Why Towers Are Made of Triangles
hook_text: Take the diagonals out of a cell phone tower and it folds like a cardboard box. Here is why.
clip_script: Stand under a cell phone tower and look up. Legs carry the weight down to a concrete block. Flat bars hold the legs apart. And slanting bars zigzag all the way up. Why the slanting bars? Take one panel: two legs, two flat bars, a rectangle. Push it sideways like the wind does and it leans into a diamond, because the corners turn and nothing has to stretch. A tower of rectangles would fall in the first storm. Add one slanting bar and the rectangle becomes two triangles. To lean now, the wind would have to stretch steel. It cannot. Locked. That is triangulation, and it is why a tower can be mostly air and still stand rigid. Look around South Africa and it is everywhere: electricity pylons across the veld, farm windmills since the 1870s, the headgear over Johannesburg's mines. Triangles, tapered, bolted down. Same lesson, three times.
visual_style: Whiteboard tower panel leaning into a parallelogram, then locked by a diagonal; pylon, wind pump and headgear silhouettes with triangles highlighted.
pacing: Slow look up the tower, quick lean-and-lock demonstration, three rapid cousins.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sketch a tower near you with every diagonal marked.
